intro: “Kuriose Geschichte” (A Curious Story) is the second piece of Schumann’s Kinderszenen, Op. 15. It is in D major and is built from clipped phrases and short flourishes, with a sudden singing line.

sections.label: A · Eight-bar theme, stated twice
sections.mNote: Two eight-bar statements, written out in full.

sections.label: B · A singing line in G major
A″ · Final return of the opening section
sections.mNote: Piano, then mezzo-forte; a ritardando closes the piece.

cues.title: Opening theme, bars 1–16
cues.text: An upbeat and two quick grace notes are followed by a short, clipped figure. Small rests break up the D major tune. At the end of each eight-bar phrase, both hands run upwards together.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, plate 6016, pp. 4–5, bars 1–16; Ying-Chun Liu’s Mutopia transcription, based on Leichte Stücke (1900). https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=355
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Contrasting phrase in G major
cues.text: Four quieter bars follow. The tune moves in even quavers over a walking bass, in G major. The clipped opening figure then returns, still marked piano.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, pp. 4–5, bars 17–21: piano, slurred phrases, G-major harmony over B at bar 17; opening figure returns at bar 21.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Letter to Clara Wieck, 1838
cues.text: Writing to Clara Wieck in March 1838, Schumann listed A Curious Story among his new pieces. “You will enjoy them,” he told her, “though of course you must forget yourself as a virtuoso.” He had chosen about twelve from thirty little pieces; thirteen reached print.
cues.evidence: Schumann to Clara Wieck, letter begun 17 March 1838, quoted in Thomas Synofzik, 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (2013), item 3. Translation from the German. The catalogue dates the letter 17 March; other editions give 19 March. https://www.schumann-zwickau.de/media/archiv-sonderausstellungen/2013_175_Jahre_Kinderszenen.pdf

transitions.title: Into the slurred piano phrase
transitions.to: B · A singing line in G major
transitions.how: The upward run reaches A. A pair of quavers leads into the new phrase, marked piano, with G in the melody over B in the bass at bar 17. The rests that broke up the tune stop, and both hands now play slurred lines.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 4, bars 15–20; Mutopia transcription confirms the bass B at bar 17.

transitions.title: Return of the opening, bars 20–21
transitions.from: B · A singing line in G major
transitions.how: The bass reaches D and rises through D♯ to E. Above it, the upbeat and grace notes of the opening return in D major. The opening was marked mezzo-forte, and this return is marked piano.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, pp. 4–5, bars 20–21; bass pitches checked against the Mutopia transcription.

transitions.title: Ritardando to the D major cadence
transitions.how: In bars 27–30 the tune rises to F♯, slows under a ritardando and falls to D over a D major cadence. A quaver upbeat brings back the slurred passage, with G over B in the following bar. The left hand keeps up its movement throughout.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 5, bars 27–30: ritardando, D-major cadence and return of the slurred passage.

transitions.title: Return of the opening in D major
transitions.to: A″ · Final return of the opening section
transitions.how: The bass climbs D–D♯–E again, and grace notes lead into the last statement of the opening in D major. Schumann marks it piano, raises it to mezzo-forte in its second half and writes a ritardando over the final descent to D.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 5, bars 32–40; piano at the return, mezzo-forte in its second half, ritardando at the close.

composer.epithet: Composer and music critic, a bookseller’s son, whose piano music depicts lovers, masks and arguments.
facts: Friedrich Wieck, piano; Heinrich Dorn, composition
Co-founded the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik in 1834; edited it until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
composer.background:
Robert Schumann grew up among books in Zwickau. His father August sold and published them, and encouraged his son’s music; Robert read Jean Paul’s novels while learning the piano. The novels contain twins, disguises, and conversations that wander from their subject and return to it unexpectedly. In Papillons, his early set of piano dances, Schumann took up the masked ball at the end of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre.

He went to Leipzig to study law in 1828 and moved to Heidelberg the following year. In the end he persuaded his mother to let him pursue music. Friedrich Wieck undertook to train him as a pianist. Wieck’s young daughter Clara was already performing in public; Robert was the older pupil and had more ground to make up. By 1832 paralysis in his right hand had ended his hopes of becoming a virtuoso. He studied composition with Heinrich Dorn and turned to composing and writing.
